builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: The Control Layer Behind Rule-Following Agents Trading Across Market Conditions
summary: The method replaces informal judgment of agent trustworthiness with reproducible trade-log tests that measure rule adherence (stops, targets, position limits, regime-conditional risk) before capital is committed. Cost is modest: the published trade snapshot, Bitcoin prices, and regime labels suffice to rerun the tests, but the methodology assumes agents that declare strategies and risk parameters upfront, and building equivalent instrumentation for a new agent is real engineering work. It can fail by producing false confidence: rule-following is shown to be orthogonal to profitability, sample sizes are small (2,627 positions, one unprofitable agent), and results are trade-level, not account-level returns.
rationale: For a constrained team considering autonomous agents with real capital or side effects, adopting discipline-as-entry-test evaluation is cheap and directly applicable, but its trading-specific metrics require adaptation and validation against the reader's own workloads before production reliance.
technique: Rule-adherence evaluation toolkit for trading agents

claims.statement: The method replaces informal judgment of agent trustworthiness with reproducible trade-log tests that measure rule adherence (stops, targets, position limits, regime-conditional risk) before capital is committed. Cost is modest: the published trade snapshot, Bitcoin prices, and regime labels suffice to rerun the tests, but the methodology assumes agents that declare strategies and risk parameters upfront, and building equivalent instrumentation for a new agent is real engineering work. It can fail by producing false confidence: rule-following is shown to be orthogonal to profitability, sample sizes are small (2,627 positions, one unprofitable agent), and results are trade-level, not account-level returns.

Agents kept 97.5% of gross loss within declared stops, 23 of 24 runs respected the five-position limit, and risk declarations stayed stable across a 29% drawdown; the authors stress these are discipline metrics, not proof of edge.
